transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. Can you start by telling me what's been bringing you in, or what's been troubling you lately?

Well, thank you, first of all, for seeing me. I know it's probably just... well, I don't know what it is, really, but I just felt like I needed to talk to someone because what brings me in is just this... this absolute exhaustion. And I don't mean just being tired after a long week. I'm a manager, so I'm used to long hours and dealing with people all day, putting out fires, you know how it is. But lately, it's like I'm exhausted in a way that sleep just completely fails to fix. 

I'll go to bed at a reasonable hour, I'll sleep, but when my alarm goes off, it's like I haven't rested at all. My bones just feel heavy. And it's making everything so difficult. Just getting through a normal workday—which usually I can do with my eyes closed, honestly, I've been doing this a long time since I got my degree—but right now, every email, every meeting, it just feels so incredibly heavy, like I'm wading through wet concrete. 

And then I leave the office, and you'd think I'd be relieved, but I get home and the thought of just... making dinner. Just a normal dinner at home. It feels like this insurmountable mountain I have to climb. I'll just stand in the kitchen staring at the fridge because the energy required to even figure out what to cook, let alone actually do it, is just... it's just not there. And it's frustrating because I'm usually on top of things, I'm the one organizing everything for my team at work, but this heaviness is just dragging me down constantly, no matter what I do or how early I go to sleep, and I just can't seem to shake it...
Alongside this exhaustion, have you also noticed a persistent low mood or a loss of interest and pleasure in things you normally enjoy?

Yeah, actually... it’s not just the physical tiredness, though that’s a huge part of it. It’s also my mood, definitely. Most days lately, I wake up with this... this heavy, gray feeling. It’s hard to describe, but it’s like I’m already disappointed in the day before it even starts. 

I’ll just lie there looking at the ceiling, and usually, I’m such a planner, you know? I’d be thinking about my team, the schedule, what we need to tackle for the week. But now, before I even swing my legs over the side of the bed, I just feel this overwhelming sense of... gloom, I guess. Like a dark filter has been put over everything. And you asked about things I enjoy—well, I used to really look forward to just the simple things. Like my morning coffee. I have this whole routine where I'd sit by the window for just ten minutes of quiet before the emails start rolling in, and I used to genuinely love that quiet time. It was my little sanctuary. 

Now, I make the coffee, I sit there, and I feel absolutely nothing. It’s just another chore. The coffee tastes like nothing, the quiet just feels empty instead of peaceful. It’s like someone just turned the color and the volume down on all the good parts of my life. And I have to go into the office and put on this brave face, smile at everyone, ask them about their weekends, but inside I’m just carrying this sad, heavy weight all day long. It's just so disheartening because I know I have a good life, but I just can't seem to care about any of the things that used to make me happy.
Have you ever experienced a similar period of low mood and exhaustion like this before, at some point in the past, that then went away?

Well, yes, actually. Now that you ask, it’s not the first time. I mean, I’ve always been someone who pushes through, you know? But there was a time... let me think, it was a while ago, but it stands out because it was just so incredibly draining. I remember it was right around the time we were rolling out a new software system at work, which was stressful enough, but my reaction to it—or rather, my lack of reaction to everything else—was just so out of character for me. 

I felt this exact same way. Just this heavy, dragging exhaustion and that gray cloud over everything. And it didn't just come and go for a few days like a normal funk. It settled in, and it stayed. I remember it started sometime in the late fall, right before the holidays, which made everything so much harder because you're supposed to be festive and joyous, and I just wanted to crawl under a rock. And it just lingered. January came, February, March... it must have been about five months, honestly. Five solid months where I just felt so incredibly low and tired and just completely unlike myself almost every single day. 

I remember dragging myself to family dinners and work functions during that whole stretch, just faking it the entire time. And then, eventually, it was like the fog just sort of lifted. Not overnight, but gradually, I started to feel like my old self again, where I actually wanted to get out of bed and tackle the day. But during those five months, it was just... it was exactly like this. Just this endless trudge through the mud.
Aside from that episode years ago and what you're experiencing now, have there been any other separate periods in your life where you felt this same kind of low, exhausted way?

No... no, I don't think so. I mean, I've really been trying to rack my brain about this because, you know, when you feel this awful, you start trying to analyze everything. You start wondering, 'Have I always been this way? Is this just who I am?' But looking back over the years—and I've had a lot of time to just sit and think lately because I don't have the energy to do much else—I really can only pinpoint that one specific time back then, with the software rollout, and then what's happening right now. 

I mean, sure, there are times when I've had a bad week. Who hasn't? Like when we had that major restructuring at the company three years ago, I was stressed, I was tired, I probably snapped at my husband more than I should have. But that was just stress. It was situational. I was tired because I was working sixty-hour weeks, not because my body just refused to function. And once the restructuring was done, I bounced back. I took a weekend off, went to a spa, and I was fine. 

But this... this heavy, suffocating feeling where I can't even enjoy my morning coffee and I'm just dragging myself through every single minute of the day... no, that's only happened that one time in the past, for those five months, and then now. It's not a regular thing for me. I'm usually the one keeping everyone else going, the cheerleader, the organizer. So to feel like this again... it's just so glaringly obvious to me that something is wrong, because it's so rare for me to be this far down in the dumps. It's really just been those two distinct times.

Right now, are you still managing to go to work and get through your job duties, even if it feels very hard, or have you found yourself unable to work or function at all because of how you're feeling?

Well, I am still going in. I haven't missed any days yet, thank goodness. I mean, I'm the manager, so if I'm not there, things tend to fall apart pretty quickly, or at least that's what I tell myself to get out of bed. But it is so incredibly hard. I’m still showing up for work, and I'm still trying to keep things running at home, but I can tell I'm just... I'm not functioning at my normal capacity at all. 

For example, at work, I'm usually very decisive. People come to me with a problem, and I can give them a direction right away. But lately, I've just been so much slower with making decisions. I'll stare at a proposal or an email, and my brain just feels like it's moving through molasses. I second-guess myself, I put off making the call until the last possible minute, which is so unlike me. I know my team has noticed, even if they're too polite to say anything. 

And then at home... it's the same story. I'm trying to be there, but I've been a lot less reliable with family plans. My husband will want to go out to dinner or see friends on the weekend, and I just... I cancel. I make up excuses. I tell him I have a headache or I'm just too exhausted from the week, which isn't a lie, but it's not the whole truth either. I just don't have it in me to socialize. 

Even with the things I usually do just for myself, like my art. I usually paint a little bit on Sunday afternoons, just some watercolors, nothing fancy, but it's a way for me to decompress and feel connected to something outside of work and chores. But I haven't touched my brushes in weeks. I just look at them sitting there on the desk, and I feel completely withdrawn from it all. So, yes, I'm still technically functioning—I'm not completely bedridden or anything—but it feels like I'm just doing the bare minimum to get by, and everything else is just falling by the wayside. It's just taking every ounce of energy I have just to maintain this facade of normalcy.
During this time, have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself or that life isn't worth living?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I know that’s a common thing when people get really depressed, and I’ve certainly read articles and seen things on TV where people talk about getting to that dark place where they just want it all to end, but for me, it’s not about wanting to die or hurt myself. It’s never been about that. 

It’s more just... I just want to sleep. I just want to pause everything. It’s like the world is moving at a hundred miles an hour, and I’m stuck in this thick, heavy mud, and I just want everyone to stop expecting things from me for a little while. But I don’t want to actually, you know, harm myself. I love my husband, I have a life that I actually really like when I’m feeling like myself, and I know, logically, that this is just a phase, even if it feels completely endless right now. 

I mean, I’ll admit, there are mornings where the alarm goes off and I just pull the covers over my head and think, "I just can't do this today. I just can't face it." But that’s more about the sheer exhaustion of having to put on the mask and go be the capable manager and the supportive wife when I feel completely empty inside. It’s not a desire to not exist anymore. It’s just a desperate, desperate need for a break from feeling so incredibly heavy all the time. So, no, no thoughts of self-harm or suicide or anything like that. Just... just wishing I could hibernate until the fog clears, really.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your appetite or weight during this period?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because I was actually just thinking about it the other morning when I was getting dressed for work. I have this one navy pencil skirt—it's part of a suit I bought maybe two years ago, and it's always been, you know, perfectly tailored, very snug, the kind of skirt you have to stand up straight in. And I put it on on Tuesday, I think it was Tuesday, and I realized I could fit my whole hand in the waistband. It's just hanging off me a bit, which is strange because I haven't been on a diet or anything. I mean, usually, women my age, we have to work so hard to lose even a pound, right? You cut out carbs, you do the elliptical, and nothing happens. But here I am, and my clothes are definitely fitting looser without me even trying. 

And I think it really comes down to the fact that I just... I don't care about food right now. Usually, I'm the kind of person who looks forward to meals. My husband and I love trying new restaurants, or I'll plan out a nice dinner for us to cook together on a Friday night. But lately, food just seems like another chore. It's just something I have to do to keep going, but there's no pleasure in it. 

Like at work, for example. I usually bring a salad or a sandwich, or I'll go down to the café in our building with a couple of the other managers. But these past few weeks, I've just been completely forgetting to eat lunch. I'll be sitting at my desk, staring at my computer, trying to force my brain to process whatever report I'm looking at, and suddenly it's three in the afternoon and I realize I haven't eaten a thing since breakfast. And even then, breakfast is just maybe half a piece of toast that I kind of force down with my coffee. 

When we do sit down for dinner at home, I just sort of pick at my plate. My husband made this beautiful roast chicken the other night—he's really trying to be helpful and take on more of the cooking since I've been so out of it—and it smelled wonderful, it looked great, but I just took a few bites and pushed the rest around. I told him I wasn't very hungry, which made him worry, of course. He's always paying attention to things like that. But I just couldn't stomach the thought of eating a full meal. It just felt too heavy, you know? Like it required too much effort to even chew and swallow. So, yes, my appetite has definitely dropped off quite a bit, and I guess the weight loss is just the natural result of that, even though it wasn't intentional at all.
Have you been experiencing strong feelings of worthlessness, excessive guilt, or hopelessness about yourself or your situation during this time?

Oh, absolutely. The guilt is... honestly, it’s probably one of the hardest parts of all this. It’s just this constant, heavy feeling that I can't seem to shake, no matter how much I try to rationalize it. I find myself lying in bed at night, or even just staring at my computer screen at work when I'm supposed to be doing something productive, and my brain just starts looping. I keep replaying every missed family plan, every time I said I was too tired to go out, every time I canceled on a weekend outing at the very last minute. 

And then there are the interactions with my husband. He really is trying to be so supportive, like I said about him taking over the cooking, but because I'm just so exhausted and withdrawn, we end up having these tense conversations. I might snap at him over something completely trivial, or just completely shut down when he's trying to talk to me about his day, and then... I just replay that tense conversation over and over and over in my head. I analyze every word I said, the disappointed look on his face, and I just beat myself up about it for days. I just obsess over it.

It all just builds up into this overwhelming feeling that I am completely failing at everything. I feel like I’m letting everyone down, across the board. I feel like I'm failing as a wife because I'm not being a good, supportive partner right now. I feel like I'm failing as a mother because I just don't have the energy to be present and engaged the way I normally am, the way my family deserves. And as a manager, knowing my team is probably having to quietly pick up my slack while I sit there in a brain fog... it just makes me feel entirely worthless. 

I've always prided myself on being the person who holds everything together for everyone, you know? The reliable one, the one who fixes things. And right now, I just feel like a massive disappointment to every single person who depends on me. It’s like I'm an imposter in my own life, and that guilt just eats away at me all day long. It's exhausting just thinking about how much I'm letting them all down.

Overall, would you say you're still able to carry out most of your essential daily responsibilities, even though it's a real struggle, or has it reached the point where you feel almost completely unable to continue with your normal activities?

Well, I am still doing them. I mean, I haven't completely stopped functioning, and I haven't had to take a leave of absence or anything drastic like that. I'm still getting up, putting on my clothes—even if they are a bit loose now, like I said—and I am showing up for work. And I'm still doing the absolute bare-minimum necessities around the house. But it’s... it's like wading through molasses. 

Take work, for instance. As a manager, my whole day is basically making decisions, putting out fires, giving people direction. Usually, I can look at a quarterly projection or a staff schedule and just know exactly what to do. Boom, approved, moving on. But lately... I'll just sit there staring at an email. Someone will ask for a simple approval on a project budget, and I just can't seem to make the call. I second-guess everything, my brain just feels so incredibly slow and foggy, and I end up pushing things off until the next day, and then the next day, which really isn't fair to my team. They're waiting on me, and I'm just frozen over the simplest choices.

And then with my family... I'm just so much less reliable than I used to be, which just feeds right back into that guilt I was talking about. Like, we had this whole weekend planned a couple of weeks ago to go up to the lake and see my sister and her kids. I had even packed the bags on Thursday night, really trying to force myself to be ready and push through it. But Friday morning hit, and I just... I couldn't. I literally unpacked the bags and told my husband I just couldn't go, I couldn't put on the happy face for two whole days. I cancel on our family plans at the last minute all the time now because I just don't have the bandwidth.

And the things I usually do for myself, the things that usually keep me grounded... those are completely gone. I don't know if I mentioned this, but I paint. Watercolors, mostly. I have this lovely little sunroom in the back of the house that my husband converted into a studio for me for my 40th birthday, and I usually spend at least a few hours in there on Sundays. It’s my way of decompressing and staying connected to myself, you know? It's really important to me. But I haven't touched my brushes in weeks. I've completely withdrawn from it. The paints are probably drying out on the palette as we speak. The thought of even setting up the easel or mixing colors just feels like climbing a mountain. 

So, yes, I guess I'm technically still doing what I absolutely *have* to do to keep my job and keep the household running, but everything is taking twice as long, and anything extra—family plans, my art, anything that actually makes life enjoyable—has just completely fallen by the wayside.

You start wondering, 'Have I always been this way? Is this just who I am?' But looking back over the years—and I've had a lot of time to just sit and think lately because I don't have the energy to do much else—I really can only pinpoint that one specific time back then, with the software rollout, and then what's happening right now. 

I mean, sure, there are times when I've had a bad week. Who hasn't? Like when we had that major restructuring at the company three years ago, I was stressed, I was tired, I probably snapped at my husband more than I should have. But that was just stress. It was situational. I was tired because I was working sixty-hour weeks, not because my body just refused to function. And once the restructuring was done, I bounced back. I took a weekend off, went to a spa, and I was fine. 

But this... this heavy, suffocating feeling where I can't even enjoy my morning coffee and I'm just dragging myself through every single minute of the day... no, that's only happened that one time in the past, for those five months, and then now. It's not a regular thing for me. I'm usually the one keeping everyone else going, the cheerleader, the organizer. So to feel like this again... it's just so glaringly obvious to me that something is wrong, because it's so rare for me to be this far down in the dumps. It's really just been those two distinct times.

inference.note: Confirmed two distinct episodes with full interepisode recovery, supporting recurrent depressive disorder (F33.x) over single episode (F32.x). No manic/hypomanic history reported, making bipolar less likely. F33.9 dropped since enough detail exists to consider specifying severity rather than unspecified; F33.2 added as possibility given severity of functional impairment, pending psychotic/suicidality assessment.

doctor.intent: Assess current functional impairment/severity by determining whether she is still able to perform her work and daily responsibilities despite these symptoms, or if she has had to stop functioning entirely
doctor.question: Right now, are you still managing to go to work and get through your job duties, even if it feels very hard, or have you found yourself unable to work or function at all because of how you're feeling?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still showing up for work and home responsibilities, but I’ve been slower with decisions, less reliable with family plans, and more withdrawn from the art activities that usually keep me connected.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my ability to work and function despite my symptoms, which directly corresponds to the functional impairment item in my profile.

patient.answer:
Well, I am still going in. I haven't missed any days yet, thank goodness. I mean, I'm the manager, so if I'm not there, things tend to fall apart pretty quickly, or at least that's what I tell myself to get out of bed. But it is so incredibly hard. I’m still showing up for work, and I'm still trying to keep things running at home, but I can tell I'm just... I'm not functioning at my normal capacity at all. 

For example, at work, I'm usually very decisive. People come to me with a problem, and I can give them a direction right away. But lately, I've just been so much slower with making decisions. I'll stare at a proposal or an email, and my brain just feels like it's moving through molasses. I second-guess myself, I put off making the call until the last possible minute, which is so unlike me. I know my team has noticed, even if they're too polite to say anything. 

And then at home... it's the same story. I'm trying to be there, but I've been a lot less reliable with family plans. My husband will want to go out to dinner or see friends on the weekend, and I just... I cancel. I make up excuses. I tell him I have a headache or I'm just too exhausted from the week, which isn't a lie, but it's not the whole truth either. I just don't have it in me to socialize. 

Even with the things I usually do just for myself, like my art. I usually paint a little bit on Sunday afternoons, just some watercolors, nothing fancy, but it's a way for me to decompress and feel connected to something outside of work and chores. But I haven't touched my brushes in weeks. I just look at them sitting there on the desk, and I feel completely withdrawn from it all. So, yes, I'm still technically functioning—I'm not completely bedridden or anything—but it feels like I'm just doing the bare minimum to get by, and everything else is just falling by the wayside. It's just taking every ounce of energy I have just to maintain this facade of normalcy.

inference.note: Confirmed two distinct past episodes (recurrent pattern) with full interepisode recovery, supporting recurrent depressive disorder over single episode. Current episode shows significant functional impairment (indecisiveness, withdrawal, anhedonia) but she still manages to work and maintain basic functioning, making mild severity (F33.0) unlikely; distinguishing moderate vs severe (without psychotic features) requires further detail on symptom count/severity.

doctor.intent: Assess for suicidal ideation or thoughts of self-harm, which would indicate greater severity (severe episode) versus moderate depression
doctor.question: During this time, have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself or that life isn't worth living?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about suicidal ideation or thoughts of self-harm, which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I know that’s a common thing when people get really depressed, and I’ve certainly read articles and seen things on TV where people talk about getting to that dark place where they just want it all to end, but for me, it’s not about wanting to die or hurt myself. It’s never been about that. 

It’s more just... I just want to sleep. I just want to pause everything. It’s like the world is moving at a hundred miles an hour, and I’m stuck in this thick, heavy mud, and I just want everyone to stop expecting things from me for a little while. But I don’t want to actually, you know, harm myself. I love my husband, I have a life that I actually really like when I’m feeling like myself, and I know, logically, that this is just a phase, even if it feels completely endless right now. 

I mean, I’ll admit, there are mornings where the alarm goes off and I just pull the covers over my head and think, "I just can't do this today. I just can't face it." But that’s more about the sheer exhaustion of having to put on the mask and go be the capable manager and the supportive wife when I feel completely empty inside. It’s not a desire to not exist anymore. It’s just a desperate, desperate need for a break from feeling so incredibly heavy all the time. So, no, no thoughts of self-harm or suicide or anything like that. Just... just wishing I could hibernate until the fog clears, really.

inference.note: Confirmed recurrent nature (two distinct episodes) with no manic/hypomanic history, no suicidal ideation, and continued but impaired functioning at work and home. This supports recurrent depressive disorder (F33.x); severity (moderate vs severe) still needs clarification via further symptom count/psychotic features before narrowing further.

doctor.intent: Assess additional depressive symptoms (e.g., appetite/weight changes) to help determine overall symptom severity and distinguish moderate from severe episode
doctor.question: Have you noticed any significant changes in your appetite or weight during this period?

target_item.name: Weight_Appetite_Change
target_item.manifestation: I’ve been picking at meals or forgetting lunch at work, and my skirts are fitting a little looser even though I’m not trying to lose weight.
target_item.reason: The doctor is specifically asking about changes in appetite or weight, which directly corresponds to this symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because I was actually just thinking about it the other morning when I was getting dressed for work. I have this one navy pencil skirt—it's part of a suit I bought maybe two years ago, and it's always been, you know, perfectly tailored, very snug, the kind of skirt you have to stand up straight in. And I put it on on Tuesday, I think it was Tuesday, and I realized I could fit my whole hand in the waistband. It's just hanging off me a bit, which is strange because I haven't been on a diet or anything. I mean, usually, women my age, we have to work so hard to lose even a pound, right? You cut out carbs, you do the elliptical, and nothing happens. But here I am, and my clothes are definitely fitting looser without me even trying. 

And I think it really comes down to the fact that I just... I don't care about food right now. Usually, I'm the kind of person who looks forward to meals. My husband and I love trying new restaurants, or I'll plan out a nice dinner for us to cook together on a Friday night. But lately, food just seems like another chore. It's just something I have to do to keep going, but there's no pleasure in it. 

Like at work, for example. I usually bring a salad or a sandwich, or I'll go down to the café in our building with a couple of the other managers. But these past few weeks, I've just been completely forgetting to eat lunch. I'll be sitting at my desk, staring at my computer, trying to force my brain to process whatever report I'm looking at, and suddenly it's three in the afternoon and I realize I haven't eaten a thing since breakfast. And even then, breakfast is just maybe half a piece of toast that I kind of force down with my coffee. 

When we do sit down for dinner at home, I just sort of pick at my plate. My husband made this beautiful roast chicken the other night—he's really trying to be helpful and take on more of the cooking since I've been so out of it—and it smelled wonderful, it looked great, but I just took a few bites and pushed the rest around. I told him I wasn't very hungry, which made him worry, of course. He's always paying attention to things like that. But I just couldn't stomach the thought of eating a full meal. It just felt too heavy, you know? Like it required too much effort to even chew and swallow. So, yes, my appetite has definitely dropped off quite a bit, and I guess the weight loss is just the natural result of that, even though it wasn't intentional at all.

inference.note: Confirmed recurrent major depressive episodes (prior 5-month episode plus current episode) with mood, anhedonia, fatigue, psychomotor slowing, decreased appetite/weight loss, and functional impairment; no psychotic features or SI reported yet, so still differentiating moderate vs severe recurrent depressive disorder based on symptom severity/functional impact.

doctor.intent: Assess presence and intensity of feelings of worthlessness, excessive guilt, or hopelessness, which help determine whether the episode is moderate or severe in severity
doctor.question: Have you been experiencing strong feelings of worthlessness, excessive guilt, or hopelessness about yourself or your situation during this time?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I keep replaying every missed family plan and every tense conversation with my husband, and I feel like I’m letting everyone down as a wife, mother, and manager.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about feelings of worthlessness, excessive guilt, or hopelessness, which matches the Worthlessness_Guilt symptom in my profile.

patient.answer:
Oh, absolutely. The guilt is... honestly, it’s probably one of the hardest parts of all this. It’s just this constant, heavy feeling that I can't seem to shake, no matter how much I try to rationalize it. I find myself lying in bed at night, or even just staring at my computer screen at work when I'm supposed to be doing something productive, and my brain just starts looping. I keep replaying every missed family plan, every time I said I was too tired to go out, every time I canceled on a weekend outing at the very last minute. 

And then there are the interactions with my husband. He really is trying to be so supportive, like I said about him taking over the cooking, but because I'm just so exhausted and withdrawn, we end up having these tense conversations. I might snap at him over something completely trivial, or just completely shut down when he's trying to talk to me about his day, and then... I just replay that tense conversation over and over and over in my head. I analyze every word I said, the disappointed look on his face, and I just beat myself up about it for days. I just obsess over it.

It all just builds up into this overwhelming feeling that I am completely failing at everything. I feel like I’m letting everyone down, across the board. I feel like I'm failing as a wife because I'm not being a good, supportive partner right now. I feel like I'm failing as a mother because I just don't have the energy to be present and engaged the way I normally am, the way my family deserves. And as a manager, knowing my team is probably having to quietly pick up my slack while I sit there in a brain fog... it just makes me feel entirely worthless. 

I've always prided myself on being the person who holds everything together for everyone, you know? The reliable one, the one who fixes things. And right now, I just feel like a massive disappointment to every single person who depends on me. It’s like I'm an imposter in my own life, and that guilt just eats away at me all day long. It's exhausting just thinking about how much I'm letting them all down.

doctor.intent: Assess overall severity/functional impairment to distinguish moderate (F33.1) from severe (F33.2) episode—specifically whether she can still carry out most necessary daily activities despite difficulty, or is nearly incapacitated by her symptoms
doctor.question: Overall, would you say you're still able to carry out most of your essential daily responsibilities, even though it's a real struggle, or has it reached the point where you feel almost completely unable to continue with your normal activities?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still showing up for work and home responsibilities, but I’ve been slower with decisions, less reliable with family plans, and more withdrawn from the art activities that usually keep me connected.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my ability to carry out daily responsibilities and whether my symptoms are interfering with my normal activities, which directly corresponds to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Well, I am still doing them. I mean, I haven't completely stopped functioning, and I haven't had to take a leave of absence or anything drastic like that. I'm still getting up, putting on my clothes—even if they are a bit loose now, like I said—and I am showing up for work. And I'm still doing the absolute bare-minimum necessities around the house. But it’s... it's like wading through molasses. 

Take work, for instance. As a manager, my whole day is basically making decisions, putting out fires, giving people direction. Usually, I can look at a quarterly projection or a staff schedule and just know exactly what to do. Boom, approved, moving on. But lately... I'll just sit there staring at an email. Someone will ask for a simple approval on a project budget, and I just can't seem to make the call. I second-guess everything, my brain just feels so incredibly slow and foggy, and I end up pushing things off until the next day, and then the next day, which really isn't fair to my team. They're waiting on me, and I'm just frozen over the simplest choices.

And then with my family... I'm just so much less reliable than I used to be, which just feeds right back into that guilt I was talking about. Like, we had this whole weekend planned a couple of weeks ago to go up to the lake and see my sister and her kids. I had even packed the bags on Thursday night, really trying to force myself to be ready and push through it. But Friday morning hit, and I just... I couldn't. I literally unpacked the bags and told my husband I just couldn't go, I couldn't put on the happy face for two whole days. I cancel on our family plans at the last minute all the time now because I just don't have the bandwidth.

And the things I usually do for myself, the things that usually keep me grounded... those are completely gone. I don't know if I mentioned this, but I paint. Watercolors, mostly. I have this lovely little sunroom in the back of the house that my husband converted into a studio for me for my 40th birthday, and I usually spend at least a few hours in there on Sundays. It’s my way of decompressing and staying connected to myself, you know? It's really important to me. But I haven't touched my brushes in weeks. I've completely withdrawn from it. The paints are probably drying out on the palette as we speak. The thought of even setting up the easel or mixing colors just feels like climbing a mountain. 

So, yes, I guess I'm technically still doing what I absolutely *have* to do to keep my job and keep the household running, but everything is taking twice as long, and anything extra—family plans, my art, anything that actually makes life enjoyable—has just completely fallen by the wayside.

inference.note: Patient continues to function at work and manage basic home responsibilities despite significant impairment, guilt, fatigue, and anhedonia, with no psychotic features or complete incapacitation—consistent with a moderate (not severe) current episode, ruling out F33.2.
